title: Clearing Up Misconceptions Of The Letter-Home Consequence
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin clears up confusion around the optional letter-home consequence in the SCM elementary plan, arguing it is powerful precisely because it forces a misbehaving student to personally present and explain their conduct to their own parents. He frames it as a strategy that only works under a specific set of conditions -- teacher experience, an established reputation, clear rules, and proper setup at back-to-school night -- and warns that skipping those conditions turns it into a discipline disaster involving angry parents and administrator visits. He offers frequency as a diagnostic: a teacher sending only a handful of letters a year is likely doing it right, while frequent letters or letters that never come back signal a condition hasn't been met. The piece closes by reaffirming the underlying rationale: parents have a right to know when a child has chosen to misbehave repeatedly after clearly understanding the rules.
points: The letter-home consequence is optional within the elementary plan and should only be used once a teacher meets specific trust and experience conditions.
A workable benchmark is sending only a handful of letters per year; frequent letters suggest a condition is being violated.
If a letter doesn't come back signed, it almost always means one of the underlying conditions hasn't been met.
Until confident in the conditions, teachers can substitute a direct phone call or email to parents instead of the letter.
quotes: Done right, a thrice-misbehaving student must present and then articulate to their parents their rule-breaking behavior.
There are conditions that must be met. Otherwise, it can be a disaster. You could get angry complaints from parents, letters torn up and thrown away, and a visit from your administrator.
When I used the strategy for 12 years as an elementary teacher, I’d send a half dozen or so a year.
Another bad sign is if you don’t get a letter back. In every case, this because of one of the conditions above hasn’t been adequately met.
The most effective, honest, and responsible way to do this is to through a non-judgemental form letter the misbehaving but now contrite student must give their parents
